en.note:
The idea

As in English, there are two distances: this (near) and that (far). But in Dutch the form doesn't just depend on singular or plural: it depends on the noun's article, de or het, just like welk/welke and ons/onze.

The table

this / thesethat / those
de-wordsdeze stoeldie stoel
het-wordsdit huisdat huis
pluraldeze stoelendie stoelen

A memory aid: the forms ending in -e (deze, die) go with de; the forms ending in -t (dit, dat) go with het. In the plural all nouns take de, so they also take deze/die: dit huis → deze huizen.

Demonstrative instead of the article

The demonstrative replaces the article, as in English: de broek → deze broek (these pants). Careful: de broek is singular in Dutch, even though English says "pants" or "trousers": deze broek is.

Dit is… / Dat zijn…: pointing things out

To introduce or point something out with zijn (is / are), you always use dit or dat, whatever the noun, even in the plural. English says "These are my children", but Dutch keeps dit; it's the verb that agrees:

  • Dit is mijn broer. (This is my brother.)
  • Dit zijn mijn kinderen. (These are my children.)
  • Dat zijn mijn schoenen. (Those are my shoes.)

This or that?

deze/dit for what's near the speaker (often with hier), die/dat for what's farther away (often with daar): Deze trui is mooi, maar die trui is lelijk.

dat is also used to refer to something just said, like English "that": Dat weet ik niet. (I don't know that.)

Time words

With time words you use deze/dit for the current period: deze week (this week), dit jaar (this year).

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Forgetting to check de/het: dit stoel → deze stoel (de stoel).
  • Using dit/dat before a plural noun: dat boeken → die boeken.
  • Translating "These are…" word for word: Deze zijn mijn kinderen → Dit zijn mijn kinderen.
  • Leaving the verb singular: Dat is mijn schoenen → Dat zijn mijn schoenen.
  • Keeping the article too: deze de broek → deze broek.
en.vlaams: In spoken Flemish you often hear da instead of dat ("da's goed", "da weet ik nie"); in some areas also dees instead of deze. In Belgium a dress shirt is called het hemd; in the Netherlands people usually say het overhemd.
